levels.title: Lighthouse Keeper's Toolkit
levels.story: The lighthouse keeper's tool shed is a mess, and every islander needs a different way to store things. Match each islander to the right tool, then help run the busy evening shift.

hook.question: Press undo three times in any app, and it takes back your last three changes, newest first. It never undoes your oldest change first. How does the app keep them in the right order?
hook.answer: It keeps your changes on a stack. Every change is pushed on top, and undo pops the top one off, so the newest change always comes back first. Last in, first out.

bullets: A data structure is a way of organising data so the jobs you do most often are fast. Choose one by asking: what will I do with this data most?
Array: items sit side by side, numbered from 0. Jumping to any item by its number takes one step, but squeezing an item into the middle means shifting everything after it.
Linked list: each item points to the next one. Adding or removing an item where you already are is quick, but reaching item 500 means walking past the first 499.
Stack (last in, first out): push puts an item on top, and pop takes the top item off. Think of a pile of plates.
Queue (first in, first out): enqueue joins the back of the line, and dequeue lets the front one go. Think of the ferry line.
Stacks and queues are abstract data types: they're defined by what you can do with them, not by how they're built. Either can be built on an array or a linked list.
learn.diagramCaption: A stack only lets you reach the top. A queue lets items in at the back and out at the front.

play.needsIntro: Each islander has a job to do. Pick the structure that makes their most common job quick.

needs.need: I want an undo button that always reverses my latest brush stroke first.
hints: The newest stroke has to come back out first.
Last in, first out is a stack.
needs.explain: A stack hands back the newest item first: perfect for undo.

needs.need: Whoever joined the ferry line first should board first.
hints: The person who has waited longest goes next.
First in, first out is a queue.
needs.explain: A queue serves the oldest item first: fair for a line.

needs.need: I need to jump straight to entry number 500 in my tide log, many times a day.
hints: The key job is jumping to a numbered position.
Only one of these reaches any position in a single step.
needs.explain: An array finds any numbered item in one step, because items sit side by side.

needs.need: In a long conga line, I keep adding and removing dancers right next to where I'm standing, without shuffling everyone else along.
hints: Inserting in an array means shifting everything after the gap.
When you're already at the spot, a linked list just relinks two pointers.
needs.explain: In a linked list, adding or removing next to where you are only changes a couple of links.

needs.need: Print the documents in the order people sent them.
hints: The first document sent should come out first.
That's first in, first out.
needs.explain: Print jobs wait in a queue, so they come out in the order they arrived.

play.stackIntro: Crates get stacked on the pier as boats arrive. Watch each push, and predict which crate comes off at each pop.
play.queueIntro: Passengers join the ferry line. Watch each one join, and predict who boards at each dequeue.

words.enqueue: {v} joins the back of the line.
popHints: A stack only lets you reach one end.
It's the crate pushed most recently, the one on top.
dequeueHints: A queue serves whoever has waited longest.
It's the passenger at the front of the line.

feed.prompt: Push A, push B, push C, then pop. What comes off?
feed.explain: A stack gives back the newest item first, and C went on last.

feed.prompt: Enqueue A, B, C. Dequeue twice. Who is still waiting?
feed.answer: Just C. A and B were first in, so they were first out.

feed.prompt: Why is reaching item 500 slow in a linked list, but quick in an array?

options.text: A linked list only knows where the next item is, so you walk there one link at a time
Linked lists store their items in random order
Linked lists can only hold 499 items

feed.explain: Array items sit side by side, so position 500 can be worked out directly. A list has to follow 499 links to get there.

feed.prompt: Your browser's Back button takes you to the page you visited most recently. Which structure does that behave like?
feed.explain: Most recent first is last in, first out: a stack.

feed.prompt: A stack and a queue are both "abstract data types". What does "abstract" mean here?
feed.answer: They're defined by their operations (push and pop, or enqueue and dequeue), not by how they're built. Either can be built on an array or a linked list.

fieldNotes.title: Every program runs on a stack
fieldNotes.text: When one function calls another, the computer pushes a note onto the call stack saying where to come back to. When a function finishes, its note is popped. Recursion that never stops keeps pushing until the stack runs out of room: that's a "stack overflow", the error the famous coding Q&A site is named after.

fieldNotes.title: Queues keep the internet calm
fieldNotes.text: Big apps rarely do everything the moment you tap a button. Uploading a video or sending an order usually drops a job into a message queue, and worker computers take jobs from the front in turn. If there's a sudden rush, the queue just gets longer for a while instead of the whole app crashing.
fieldNotes.verifyNote: General description of message queues; check the wording is fair. The source link is a general data structures text, not about message queues specifically.

summary: You matched each job to the structure that makes it fast: stacks for newest-first, queues for oldest-first, arrays for jumping to a position, and linked lists for adding and removing where you already are.
Then you ran a stack and a queue by hand, which is exactly how you'll trace algorithms for the rest of the archipelago.

mistake.title: Mixing up stacks and queues
mistake.text: A stack serves the newest item first. A queue serves the oldest item first. When unsure, ask: "does whoever has waited longest go next?" If yes, it's a queue.

levels.title: Growth Race
levels.story: It's regatta day, and every boat runs on a different formula. Each captain claims their boat has the gentlest climb, the one that stays cheap as the course gets longer. Time to find out who's right.

hook.question: An app runs smoothly with 100 users, then grinds to a halt with 100,000. Nobody changed the code. What changed?
hook.answer: The input size, n. If the app does about n² steps, 100 users means 10,000 steps, but 100,000 users means 10,000,000,000 steps: a million times more work for a thousand times more users. Growth rate is what decides whether code survives success.

bullets: We measure an algorithm's cost by counting basic steps (like comparisons), written as a function of the input size n.
What matters most is how fast that function grows as n gets big, not its exact value for small n.
O(g) means "grows no faster than g" (an upper bound). Ω(g) means "grows at least as fast as g" (a lower bound). Θ(g) means both: it grows at the same rate as g.
Constant factors and smaller terms don't change the growth rate: 3n² + 5n is still Θ(n²).
From gentlest to steepest: 1, log n, √n, n, n log n, n², n³, 2ⁿ, n!
Handy test: work out f(n)/g(n) as n gets huge. If it goes to 0, f grows slower. If it settles on a positive number, they grow at the same rate. If it shoots to infinity, f grows faster.
learn.diagramCaption: Steps needed as n grows. The 2ⁿ column explodes long before n gets big.

play.rankIntro: Tap the boats from the gentlest climb (slowest-growing) to the steepest.

rankItems.hint: Start with the one that doesn't grow at all.

rankItems.label: log n
rankItems.hint: Next: the one that only grows by one step each time n doubles.

rankItems.label: n
rankItems.hint: Next: the one that grows in step with n.

rankItems.label: n log n
rankItems.hint: Next: a little steeper than n, because of an extra log factor.

rankItems.label: 2ⁿ
rankItems.hint: Last: the one that doubles every time n goes up by just one.

play.rankDone: Gentlest to steepest: 1, log n, n, n log n, n², 2ⁿ.
play.raceIntro: Captain Ada's boat needs 100n steps. Captain Bo's needs n². Fewer steps is better. Predict who's ahead at each marker.
play.raceAsk: At n = {n}, whose boat needs fewer steps?
raceHints: Work out both: multiply n by 100 for Ada, and n by itself for Bo.
At n = {n}, Ada needs {a} steps and Bo needs {b}.
play.raceSay: At n = {n}: Ada needs {a} steps, Bo needs {b}.
play.raceStart: The boats line up. Nobody has moved yet.
play.raceDone: Bo looked better for small n, but n² overtakes 100n from n = 100 on. Small inputs can fool you.
play.tfIntro: Captains make bold claims. Use the f(n)/g(n) test when you're unsure.

hints: Divide by n²: (3n² + 5n)/n² = 3 + 5/n.
That settles on 3, a positive number, so they grow at the same rate.
statements.explain: True. The ratio settles on 3, so it's even Θ(n²), and Θ implies O.

hints: Divide: n²/n = n.
The ratio shoots to infinity, so n² grows faster than n.
statements.explain: False. n² outgrows n, so n can't be an upper bound for it.

hints: O is only an upper bound. It doesn't have to be tight.
n/n² = 1/n goes to 0, so n grows slower than n².
statements.explain: True. An upper bound can be loose: n grows no faster than n².

hints: Changing a log's base only multiplies it by a constant.
log₂ n = log₁₀ n / log₁₀ 2, so the ratio is a constant.
statements.explain: True. All log bases grow at the same rate.

hints: Ω means "grows at least as fast as".
(n log n)/n² = (log n)/n goes to 0, so n log n grows slower.
statements.explain: False. n log n grows slower than n², so n² isn't a lower bound for it.

hints: The ratio is exactly 2, a constant.
statements.explain: True. 2ⁿ⁺¹ is just 2 times 2ⁿ, a constant factor.

play.countTitle: Count it: find the biggest crate
play.countIntro: The harbour master scans the crates left to right, keeping the biggest one so far. Before running it, predict how many comparisons it takes.
play.countPrompt: How many comparisons to find the biggest of these 8 crates?
countHints: The first crate starts as "biggest so far" without any comparison.
Every other crate is compared once.
play.countSay: Compare {v} with the biggest so far ({m}).
play.countStart: Crate 4 starts as the biggest so far. No comparison needed yet.
play.followPrompt: So with n crates, how many comparisons does finding the biggest take?
followHints: 8 crates took 7. Guess what 16 crates would take.
Every crate after the first gets one comparison.
play.followExplain: n − 1 comparisons: double the crates, double the work. That's linear growth, Θ(n).

feed.prompt: Which grows fastest as n gets huge?
feed.explain: Exponential beats every polynomial in the end: 2ⁿ doubles each time n goes up by one.

feed.prompt: 100n against n²: from which value of n does n² need at least as many steps?
feed.answer: From n = 100. There, both need 10,000 steps. After that, n² pulls ahead fast.

feed.prompt: Why do we drop constants, like the 3 in 3n², when stating growth rates?

options.text: Constants don't change how the cost grows as n gets big

feed.explain: Double the input and 3n² still quadruples, just like n². The constant depends on the machine, while the growth rate is about the algorithm.
True. O is an upper bound, and it doesn't have to be tight.

feed.prompt: Finding the biggest of 1,000 crates by scanning them once: how many comparisons?
feed.answer: 999. Every crate after the first gets one comparison: n − 1, which is Θ(n).

feed.prompt: log₂ n and log₁₀ n: how do their growth rates compare?

options.text: The same: they differ by a constant factor

feed.explain: Changing the base only multiplies by a constant, so all logs are Θ(log n).

fieldNotes.title: A billion items: 30 seconds or 30 years
fieldNotes.text: Say a computer does a billion basic steps per second. Sorting a billion items with an n log n method takes about 30 billion steps: around 30 seconds. A method doing n² steps would need a billion billion steps: about 30 years. Same computer, same data, completely different growth rate.
fieldNotes.verifyNote: Check: log₂(10⁹) ≈ 30, so n log n ≈ 3 × 10¹⁰ steps ≈ 30 s at 10⁹ steps/s; n² = 10¹⁸ steps ≈ 10⁹ s ≈ 31.7 years.

fieldNotes.title: The chessboard of rice
fieldNotes.text: An old story: put 1 grain of rice on the first square of a chessboard, 2 on the next, 4 on the next, doubling each time. The total over all 64 squares is 2⁶⁴ − 1, about 18 quintillion grains. That's 2ⁿ growth, and it's why exponential-time algorithms are hopeless for large inputs.

summary: You ranked growth rates, watched n² overtake 100n, judged O, Ω and Θ claims with the ratio test, and counted the comparisons in a real algorithm.
Counting steps and then asking "how does this grow?" is the whole game of algorithm analysis. Every island from here on uses it.

mistake.title: Trusting small inputs
mistake.text: At n = 10, Bo's n² boat looked better than Ada's 100n. But growth rate decides the winner once n gets big. Always ask what happens as n grows, not what happens for one small example.
